Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript by Rose et al is primarily focused on the study of non-V600 BRAF mutant tumors to understand molecular mechanisms of treatment response and resistance to guide the design of more effective therapies. The authors provide data from a Phase II clinical trial designed to evaluate activity of binimetinib and encorafenib targeting MEK and BRAF, respectively, to treat non-V600 BRAF mutant disease across a wide array of tumor histologies. PDX models were established from tumor biopsies to facilitate the identification of mechanisms of resistance. Two separate lines of investigation were pursued to generate preclinical data in support of combination of binimetinib and encorafenib with a third agent to improve response. First, combination of MEK/BRAF inhibitors with a CDK4/6 inhibitor to target cell cycle progression in Class 2 BRAF mutant tumors, and second, combination of these agents with a SHP2 inhibitor to address co-occurring activating mutations in RAF1 or NRAS in Class 3 tumors were explored.
This study addresses an area of high unmet medical need since the mean overall response irrespective of class of non-V600 BRAF mutation across the entire cohort of Phase 2 patients treated with binimetinib plus encorafenib was ~6 months. Overall, the data and studies reported here lend further support for key similarities and differences between class 2 and class 3 BRAF mutants for the design of improved precision therapies. However, it is recommended that the following deficiencies be addressed to strengthen the overall impact of this study.
R3-1. The Phase 1/2 study published by Yaeger and colleagues, who also evaluated clinical activity of binimetinib/encorafenib against non-V600 BRAF tumors (Rustgi et al; Oncologist 2023), should be cited. Their findings appear to corroborate the findings of the present study.
We thank the reviewer for calling attention to this reference, we have now included a reference to this manuscript in the 2nd paragraph of the discussion section: “However, another recent clinical trial enrolled patients with activating Class 2 BRAF mutations and fusions to receive B+E. This study included 3 melanoma patients, none of whom experienced a response.33”
R3-2. Was any biopsy analysis conducted showing incomplete inhibition of ERK signaling? Since biopsies were obtained during the clinical trial, it is unclear why this was not explored, as biopsy tissue is more clinically relevant than xenografts established from a heterogeneous specimen.
We thank the reviewer for this question. We did indeed perform pre and on-treatment biopsies in some patients. However, per protocol, on-treatment biopsies were optional, and thus only a minority of patients consented to this procedure. To address this reviewer comment, we reviewed all paired pre-treatment/on-treatment biopsies, performed H&E, pERK and ERK IHC. H&E sections were interrogated by a pathologist (co-author, Dr. Zaid Saeed Kamil) to confirm adequate tumor tissue. After review, we had paired biopsies with adequate tumor tissue available from 6 patients (BVR-M-04, BVR-O-10/12/13/15/17). Unfortunately 5/6 patients had PD as best response and one patient (BVR-O-10) had SD as best response. Thus we are not able to make any associations between changes in pERK levels and clinical response. Amongst these 6 non-responders however, we did observe a significant decrease in pERK+ cells in on-treatment biopsy samples compared to pre-treatment biopsy samples. These results are included in the revised manuscript as new Figure S3d. These data confirm that we did indeed observe on-target MAPK pathway inhibition with these inhibitors in patients with Class 2 & 3 non-V600 BRAF mutations. Anecdotally (and intriguingly), we did observe higher baseline pERK levels in the tumor types that were associated with higher response rates (melanoma, biliary tract tumors, BVR-M-04/BVR-O-10; average 13.4% pERK positive cells at baseline) compared to colorectal tumors (BVR-O-12/13/15/17; average 1.7% pERK positive cells at baseline; P=0.0002 t-test). This observation indicating lower baseline MAPK activity in tumor types that are less responsive to MAPKi could in-part explain a lack of benefit from MAPK inhibitors in colorectal tumors; however, our sample size is too small to make any definitive claims in this regard.
3. Figure 1b: since BRAF/MEK inhibitor combination therapy has been reported to elicit activity against BRAF V600 mutated cholangiocarcinomas, they should be distinguished from pancreatic carcinomas as opposed to all being classified as pancreaticobiliary tumors.
Per this reviewers suggestion we have removed the patient with pancreatic cancer from the “pancreaticobiliary” tumor grouping. This patient is now included in the “other” tumor group. The updated tumor groupings are: melanoma, colorectal cancer, biliary tract tumors, and other. We have revised Figure 1b,c,e; Figure S3; and Table S1 to reflect these changes. Biliary tract cancers are a heterogenous group of tumors that include cholangiocarcinomas, gallbladder and ampullary cancers (PMID: 35032765, 37416744, 38266541, 34616513, 34300274, 24857067). Importantly, BRAF/MEK inhibitors have demonstrated efficacy in biliary tract cancers with BRAF V600E mutations (PMID: 37059834).
4. Figure 2b: Tumor growth inhibition (TGI) needs to be defined.
We determined the tumor growth inhibition (TGI) index to compare the relative tumor growth inhibition Bini+Enco treatment vs. vehicle treatment in corresponding PDXs. TGI was calculated with the following equation: 100 –(100*(AUCB+E/AUCvehicle)), where the AUC was the calculated average area under the curve of all individual tumor growth curves within that treatment group. We have updated the figure legend for Figure S4c to include this definition.
4. Figure 2b: The text states that nine PDX models were established, but there are only eight models plotted here. The conclusion that there is an indirect correlation between clinical change in target lesion vs preclinical efficacy of the PDX model established from that lesion does not appear to be justified. Five of the eight PDX models shown in this figure originated from colorectal tumors, which were the most refractory histology evaluated (5 of 6 showing clinical progression).
We did establish 9 PDX models, from BEAVER trial patients. We performed targeted panel sequencing on biopsy samples from all 9 patients and whole exome sequencing on all PDXs. We were unable to detect a BRAF mutation in one of the 9 PDX models (BVR-M-04) that we developed (Figure S4b). The BRAF mutation that was indicated on this patient’s clinical pathology report (BRAF G466E) was also not present on the patient biopsy sample when we evaluated it with the TSO500 NGS assay; however, several other gene alterations (NF1, TP53, POLE, RB1) were present in both the patient sample and the PDX sample (Figure 1c, Figure S4b). This suggests that this patient had a sub-clonal BRAF mutation detected on the clinical sample that was used to determine trial eligibility. Therefore, because this was a BRAF WT PDX, we did not test the efficacy of B+E, and we have only plotted 8 models in this graph (now Figure S4d).
We feel strongly that our conclusion that “there is an indirect correlation between the clinical change in target lesion size and the tumor growth inhibition index of the corresponding PDX” is indeed justified based on the data as presented. We do not claim that we can predict response based on this model (as we unfortunately did not develop any PDXs from patients who experienced response). We claim only that that there is inverse correlation in patient tumor growth as measured by an established standardized metric (RECIST 1.1) and PDX tumor growth inhibition with the same drug treatment. The purpose of this is analysis is to confirm that the PDXs are useful models (albeit imperfect, as are all models) for drug treatment experiments and that responses in the PDX are associated with responses in patients for the same drug treatment. This is a well-established and uncontroversial feature/benefit of using PDX models. With all that being said, we have de-emphasized this result in the main manuscript text and moved this figure from Figure 2 to Supplemental Figure 4.
5. Figure 3g: Were PDX models not available from patients testing positive for E2F/G2M gene alteration to evaluate in vivo efficacy of binimetinib/encorafenib/palbociclib?
We thank the reviewer for this question. The following BEAVER PDX models had alterations in E2F/G2M genes: BVR-M-02 (PMS2, TP53); BVR-O-13 (TP53); BVR-O-15 (TP53); BVR-O-17 (SMAD3). Of these models, we evaluated the binimetinib/encorafenib/palbociclib combination in the Class 2 BRAF mutant PDX: BVR-O-17 (Figure 4g), and in Class 3 BRAF mutant PDX: BVR-O-13 (Figure S8) PDXs, in vivo.
6. Figure 3i: Combined knockdown of CDK4 and CDK6 does not appear to potentiate cell growth inhibition mediated by binimetinib and encorafenib at the low doses (line 360).
We thank the reviewer for this comment, we agree that CDK4/6 knockdown did not potentiate cell growth inhibition mediated by low dose Bini+Enco, but CDK4/6 knockdown did potentiate cell growth inhibition mediated by high dose Bini+Enco . We have adjusted the text to more accurately reflect this observation: “Notably, the combined knockdown further potentiated cell growth inhibition mediated by B+E at high doses (Figure 3i).” (page 9)
7. Triple therapy combination (B+E+palbociclib) does not appear to be more effective than palbociclib alone against MB-231 cells (lines 367-369).
In response to this comment, we have updated Figure 4A. Indeed, at the 100nM palbociclib dose, the triple therapy was not more effective than palbociclib alone in the MDA-MB-231 cells. Multiple clonogenic experiments were performed with 25nM, 50nM and 100nM palbociclib doses and differing doses of B+E. We have updated Figure 4A with a higher Bini+Enco dose which inhibits proliferation of these cells (1000nM Enco + 200nM Bini) as well as a palbociclib dose that is effective alone (50nM). The triple therapy combination is more effective than Bini+Enco (p=0.0129) and Palbociclib alone (p < 0.0001). We limit our description of the results to the comparison between B+E and the triple therapy.
8. Figure 4e-g: added benefit of combining three agents (B+E+palbociclib) does not appear to be significantly enhanced compared to palbociclib alone. Statistics should be provided comparing those two arms in each study.
We thank the reviewer for raising this point. As all of these PDXs were derived from patients who were non-responders to bini+enco, therefore, we did not power each individual PDX study to have a sample size that would allow us to detect statistically significant differences between B+E+P and B+E or Palbo. The experiments were powered to detect statistically significant differences between B+E+P and vehicle treatments.
However, to address this reviewer’s concern, we have now compiled the results of all of the colorectal PDX models that we used to evaluate this regimen (BVR-O-04, BVR-O-12, BVR-O-13 and BVR-O-17). Here we reported the change in tumor volume and perform multiple comparison testing to evaluate the difference between B+E+P vs. vehicle (P<0.0001); B+E+P vs. B+E (P<0.01), and B+E+P vs. Palbo (P<0.05). This data is now included in the revised manuscript as Figure S8d. Additionally, we performed a similar type of analysis to compare the B+E+TNO155 tumor growth to vehicle (P<0.001), B+E (P<0.01) or TNO155 (P<0.05). This analysis is also now included in the revised manuscript as Figure S12f.
8. Figure 4e-g: The absence of meaningful tumor regressions in the triple combination arms is a concern and weakens the conclusion that the preclinical data support clinical evaluation of this combination strategy for Class 2 & 3 BRAF mutant cancers (lines 538-539).
We acknowledge that this triple therapy regimen (B+E+palbo) delayed tumor growth in all tested PDXs, but it did not elicit tumor regressions in most of these models. We did however, observe tumor regressions with B+E+palbo triple therapy in the BVR-O-10 cholangiocarcinoma model (Figure S8b). We do not agree that this finding weakens the conclusion that these preclinical data support the clinical evaluation of this combination strategy. It is important to note that many of our PDX models are derived from patients with metastatic colorectal cancer (mCRC) that were refractory to multiple chemotherapies (Table S3). In clinical trials evaluating new treatments for chemotherapy-refractory mCRC, partial responses (tumor regressions) are rare. Indeed, the response rate for the BEACON regimen (encorafenib and cetuximab) in BRAF V600E mCRC is only 21%, and despite this low response rate, this regimen provided an overall survival benefit and is a standard-of-care treatment for mCRC (PMID: 31566309). Similar results were also observed for other recently approved treatments for chemotherapy refractory mCRC. Indeed, the objective response rate for Fruquintinib was <2% (7/461 pts responded) in a randomized Phase 3 clinical trial that also demonstrated an overall survival benefit, resulting in its FDA approval for treatment refractory mCRC (PMID: 37331369). Thus, we believe that significant delays in tumor growth in PDXs provides sufficient rationale to support further clinical investigation of this regimen.
9. The weight loss seen in the triple combination studies with B+E+SHP2 inhibitor highlights the importance of carrying out preclinical evaluation of therapeutic index of novel treatment strategies, an important concept that has not been addressed anywhere in the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and we agree that this finding supports the need for preclinical studies to define potentially effective novel drug combinations prior to clinical development. However, preclinical mouse models have limited ability to predict clinical toxicities of the same regimens (PMID: 31998852). Moreover, many clinical toxicities can be mitigated with supportive medications that are not typically used in preclinical studies designed to evaluate drug efficacy. For example, we observed weight loss in these mice treated with B+E+TNO155. In the clinic, weight-loss can often result from medication-induced nausea, which can be easily managed with supportive anti-emetic medications. Thus, we do not believe that the weight loss observed in these animal studies precludes clinical evaluation of this combination. However dose-finding studies testing different treatment doses and schedules would be required in any Phase 1 study evaluating this regimen, as is typically done in early drug development studies.

FINAL REMARKS
We would again like to thank all of the reviewers and the editorial team for their careful review of this manuscript including their many helpful suggestions. We started working on this project in 2017 when we began writing the clinical trial protocol. The work described in this manuscript thus encompasses 8 years of rigorous, multidisciplinary, multi-institutional collaborative work. It includes a clinical trial, and extensive in vitro and in vivo experimentations including key functional genomics experiments. Importantly – we identified potential mechanisms of resistance in patient samples (ie. acquisition of new NRAS mutations in patients progressing on treatment with B+E) and validated – using CRISPR competition assays - that mutant NRAS mediates resistance to B+E in Class 2 BRAF mutant cancer cells. Based on these observations, we also extensively evaluated two new treatment strategies that could overcome B+E resistance that we assessed in a wide array of in vitro and in vivo models. We are very proud of the quality and potential impact of this work. We hope that the reviewers and the editorial team will agree with us and consider this substantially revised manuscript acceptable for publication in Nature Communications.
